blocks.text: You'll rarely write sift up and sift down yourself. Python, Java and C++ each ship a heap — and JavaScript doesn't, so this course writes one small class once and reuses it everywhere. Here's each language's heap, how to make it order things your way, and the traps that cost people marks.
The built-in heap in each language
The same small job in all four: put some numbers in a min-heap, then take them all out. They come out smallest first.
The names differ, the ideas don't:

blocks.code:
push              remove the top   look at the top   size           build from n values
JavaScript     heap.push(x)      heap.pop()       heap.peek()       heap.size()    Heap.from(nums)
Python heapq   heappush(h, x)    heappop(h)       h[0]              len(h)         heapify(h)  (in place)
Java           offer(x)          poll()           peek()            size()         new PriorityQueue<>(list)
C++            push(x)           pop()  (void!)   top()             size()         priority_queue<int>(v.begin(), v.end())

blocks.text: Building from n values at once is **O(n)** in all four — faster than n pushes. Java's constructor does it when given a collection, and C++'s when given a range.

JavaScript has no heap. So write one once, with a **compare** function like the one `Array.prototype.sort` takes: it returns a negative number when `a` should come out **before** `b`. The default `(a, b) => a - b` makes a min-heap; `(a, b) => b - a` makes a max-heap. **Every JavaScript solution in the rest of this course uses this class.**
It's the min-heap from the last lesson with each `<` replaced by a call to `compare`. `Heap.from(values, compare)` builds a heap from a whole array in O(n), like Python's `heapify`.
Real problems rarely want plain numbers smallest first. They want **the largest**, or **the closest point**, or **the most frequent word**. Each language changes the order differently:

items: **JavaScript** — pass a compare function: `(a, b) => b - a` for a max-heap, `(a, b) => a.dist - b.dist` to order objects by a field.

**Python** — `heapq` is a **min-heap only**. For a max-heap, push `-x` and negate what comes out. To order by a key, push **tuples** like `(priority, item)`: tuples compare element by element, so the priority decides first.
**Java** — give `PriorityQueue` a comparator: `Collections.reverseOrder()` for a max-heap, or a lambda like `(a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])`.
**C++** — `priority_queue` is a **max-heap** by default; `greater<int>` makes it a min-heap. A custom comparator answers “should `a` sit **below** `b`?” — the opposite of what most people expect.

blocks.text: One example in all four. Patients arrive with a **severity** from 1 to 9. Treat the most severe first, and break ties by **arrival order**. That's a max-heap on one field and a min-heap on the other — exactly where comparators get tricky.

blocks.alt: Five patients arrive in order 0 to 4 with severities 2, 5, 3, 5 and 1. As a heap ordered by severity, highest first, with ties going to the earlier arrival, the top is patient 1 with severity 5. Patient 3 also has severity 5 but arrived later, so it sits below. The treatment order is 1, 3, 2, 0, 4.

blocks.caption: Each push shows where the new patient settles; each pop treats whoever is on top.

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n), space O(n).** Four languages, four ways to say the same order: a compare function, negated tuples, a comparator, and a pair with a negated field.

items: **Python: `heapq` is min-only.** `heappop` always returns the **smallest**. For the largest, push `-x` and negate it back when it comes out. (Python 3.14 added `heappush_max` and `heappop_max`, but many judges run older versions — negation works everywhere.)

**Python: ties between items that can't be compared.** `(priority, task)` works until two priorities tie and Python compares the tasks — a dict or a custom object raises `TypeError`. Put a counter in the middle: `(priority, count, task)`.
**Java: `a - b` in a comparator.** It overflows for large or very negative values and silently breaks the order. Use `Integer.compare(a, b)`.

**Java: printing or looping over a `PriorityQueue`.** Iteration follows the internal **array**, not sorted order — only `poll()` hands values out in order. And `int x = heap.poll()` on an empty queue throws a `NullPointerException`.
**C++: the default is a max-heap.** `top()` or `pop()` on an empty heap is undefined behaviour, and `pop()` returns nothing — read `top()` first.
**C++: comparator direction.** The top is the element that no other element is **greater** than, judged by your comparator. So a comparator returning `a > b` gives a **min**-heap.

**JavaScript: re-sorting instead of a heap.** Sorting an array after every insert costs O(n log n) per operation. And `sort()` with no compare function sorts numbers as **text**: `[10, 9].sort()` stays `[10, 9]`.

**All of them: no decrease-key.** None of these heaps can change the priority of an item already inside. Push the item again with its new priority, and **skip stale copies** when they come out — Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm does exactly this.
Python `heapq` (min-only, on a list), Java `PriorityQueue` (min by default), C++ `priority_queue` (**max** by default). JavaScript: the small `Heap` class above.
Change the order with a compare function, negation, tuples or a comparator.
push and pop are **O(log n)**; peek is **O(1)**; building from n values at once is **O(n)**.
Ties and comparator direction are where heap bugs hide — test them.
